text: Raúl Ricardo Alfonsín (Spanish pronunciation: [raˈul alfonˈsin]; 12 March 1927 – 31 March 2009) was an Argentine lawyer and statesman who served as president of Argentina from 10 December 1983 to 8 July 1989. He was the first democratically elected president after the National Reorganization Process. Ideologically, he identified as a radical and a social democrat, serving as the leader of the Radical Civic Union (UCR) from 1983 to 1991, 1993 to 1995, and 1999 to 2001 [not verified in body]. His political approach was known as "Alfonsinism." Born in Chascomús, Buenos Aires Province, Alfonsín began his law studies at the National University of La Plata and graduated from the University of Buenos Aires at the age of 23. He was affiliated with the UCR, joining the faction of Ricardo Balbín after the party split. He was elected a deputy in the legislature of the Buenos Aires province in 1958, during the presidency of Arturo Frondizi, and a national deputy during the presidency of Arturo Umberto Illia. He opposed both sides of the Dirty War and filed several writs of Habeas corpus, requesting the freedom of victims of forced disappearances, during the National Reorganization Process. He denounced the crimes of military dictatorships in other countries and opposed the actions of both sides in the Falklands War. He became the leader of the UCR after Balbín's death and won the presidency in the 1983 elections as the Radical candidate. After being elected president, Alfonsín revoked the self-amnesty law established by the military. He established the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons to investigate the crimes committed by the military, which led to the Trial of the Juntas and resulted in the sentencing of the heads of the former regime. Discontent within the military led to the mutinies of the Carapintadas, which Alfonsín appeased with the full stop law and the law of Due Obedience. He also had conflicts with the unions, which were controlled by the opposing Justicialist Party. He resolved the Beagle conflict, increased trade with Brazil, and proposed the creation of the Contadora support group to mediate between the United States and Nicaragua. He passed the first divorce law of Argentina. He initiated the Austral plan to improve the national economy, but that plan, as well as the Spring plan, failed. The resulting hyperinflation and riots led to his party's defeat in the 1989 presidential elections, which was won by Peronist Carlos Menem. Alfonsín continued as the leader of the UCR and opposed the presidency of Carlos Menem. He initiated the Pact of Olivos with Menem to negotiate the terms for the 1994 amendment of the Argentine Constitution. Fernando de la Rúa led a faction of the UCR that opposed the pact, and eventually became president in 1999. Following de la Rúa's resignation during the December 2001 riots, Alfonsín's faction provided the support needed for the Peronist Eduardo Duhalde to be appointed president by the Congress. He died of lung cancer on 31 March 2009, at the age of 82, and was given a large state funeral. Raúl Alfonsín was born on 12 March 1927 in Chascomús, 123 km (76 mi) south of Buenos Aires. His parents, Serafín Raúl Alfonsín Ochoa and Ana María Foulkes, were shopkeepers. His father was of Galician and German descent, and his mother was the daughter of Welsh immigrant Ricardo Foulkes and Falkland Islander María Elena Ford. After elementary schooling, Alfonsín enrolled at the General San Martín Military Lyceum. Although his father disliked the military, he believed it would offer a quality education similar to a private school without the cost. Alfonsín disliked the military but this education helped him understand the military mindset. He graduated after five years as a second lieutenant and did not pursue a military career, instead beginning law studies at the National University of La Plata and completing them at the University of Buenos Aires. He was not a successful lawyer: he was frequently absent from work and in debt. He married María Lorenza Barreneche, whom he met in 1949 at a masquerade ball. They moved to Mendoza, La Plata, and returned to Chascomús. They had six sons, of whom only Ricardo Alfonsín would follow a political career. Alfonsín bought a local newspaper (El Imparcial). He joined the UCR in 1946 as a member of the Intransigent Renewal Movement, a faction that opposed the UCR's incorporation into the Democratic Union coalition. He was appointed president of the party committee in Chascomús in 1951 and elected to the city council in 1954. He was briefly detained during the government of Juan Perón's reaction to the bombing of Plaza de Mayo. The Revolución Libertadora ousted Perón from the national government; Alfonsín was again briefly detained and forced to leave his office in the city council. The UCR split into two parties: the Intransigent Radical Civic Union (UCRI), led by Arturo Frondizi, and the People's Radical Civic Union (UCRP), led by Ricardo Balbín and Crisólogo Larralde. Alfonsín did not like the split but opted to follow the UCRP. He was elected deputy for the legislature of the Buenos Aires province in 1958 on the UCRP ticket and reelected in 1962. He moved to La Plata, the capital of the province, during his tenure. President Frondizi was ousted by a military coup on 29 March 1962, which also closed the provincial legislature. Alfonsín returned to Chascomús. The UCRP prevailed over the UCRI the following year, leading to the presidency of Arturo Umberto Illia. Alfonsín was elected a national deputy and then vice president of the UCRP bloc in congress. In 1963 he was appointed president of the party committee for the province of Buenos Aires. Still in his formative years, Alfonsín held no noteworthy role in the administrations of Frondizi and Illia. Illia was deposed by a new military coup in June 1966, the Argentine Revolution. Alfonsín was detained while trying to hold a political rally in La Plata and a second time when he tried to re-open the UCRP committee. He was forced to resign as a deputy in November 1966. He was detained a third time in 1968 after a political rally in La Plata. He also wrote opinion articles in newspapers under the pseudonyms Alfonso Carrido Lura and Serafín Feijó. The Dirty War began during this time, as many guerrilla groups rejected both the right-wing military dictatorship and civil governments, preferring instead a left-wing dictatorship aligned with the Soviet Union, as in the Cuban Revolution. Alfonsín clarified in his articles that he rejected both the military dictatorship and the guerrillas, advocating for free elections. The UCRP became the UCR once more, and the UCRI was turned into the Intransigent Party. Alfonsín created the Movement for Renewal and Change within the UCR to challenge Balbín's leadership. The military dictatorship called for free elections, allowing Peronism (which had been banned since 1955) to take part. Balbín defeated Alfonsín in the primary elections but lost in the main ones. Alfonsín was elected deputy once more. Illia was invited in 1975 to a diplomatic mission to the Soviet Union; he declined and proposed Alfonsín instead. Upon his return, Alfonsín became one of the founding members of the Permanent Assembly for Human Rights. He served as the defense lawyer for Mario Roberto Santucho, leader of the ERP guerrillas, but only to carry out due process of law, not because of a genuine desire to support him. The 1976 Argentine coup d'état against President Isabel Perón started the National Reorganization Process. Alfonsín filed several Habeas corpus motions, requesting the freedom of victims of forced disappearances. The UCR stayed silent over the disappearances, but Alfonsín urged the party to protest the kidnapping of senators Hipólito Yrigoyen (nephew of the former president of the same name) and Mario Anaya. He also visited other countries, denouncing those disappearances and violations of human rights. He established the magazine Propuesta y control in 1976, one of the few magazines that criticized the military dictatorship during its early stages. The magazine was published up to 1978. His editorials were collected in 1980 in the book La cuestión argentina. Alfonsín expressed opposition to the 1982 Falklands War, criticizing the deployment of troops by both sides during the conflict. He rejected the invasion of the islands, which he considered an inevitable logistic and diplomatic failure, being one of the few politicians who opposed the war from the start. He proposed an emergency government headed by Illia, with ministers from all political parties, who would call for a ceasefire with the British and call for elections. He reasoned that the British would be magnanimous in victory if negotiating the transition with a civilian government, that all Argentine parties would be involved with such negotiations, and provide greater guarantees. The proposal did not get enough support, as Peronist Deolindo Bittel proposed another post-war scenario: electing a prime minister selected by a committee of generals and politicians, who would keep a veto power and guide the new government for at least two years. This proposal implicitly intended to remove Bignone and appoint a figure akin to the late Juan Perón, but it did not get support either because the current context did not provide any such figure that would have both support from the military and from the population. Antonio Trocolli, former leader of the Radical Congress, rejected both proposals as impracticable. The Falklands Wars were lost, and the military lifted the ban on political activities on the promise to hold elections. This was a calculated move to make the politicians focus on internal infighting, instead of blaming the military for the defeat. The plan did not work as intended, as the political parties united in a temporary coalition, the "Multipartidaria," that rejected the military attempt to control the new government and asked to speed up the elections, which were called for October 1983. The Movement for Renewal and Change organized the first political event in a stadium in the Buenos Aires suburbs. As Balbín had died in 1981, the UCR had no strong leadership at the time. Alfonsín disputed the leadership of the UCR with Carlos Contín, but was unable to pass through the complex internal regulations of the party. He made a new political rally at the Luna Park, with a success comparable to a United States presidential primary. This new rally convinced Contín, who also ambitioned to be president, that he had no chances fighting against Alfonsín in proper primary elections. Fernando de la Rúa, who would have run in the primary elections against him, declined his candidacy because of Alfonsín's huge popularity. Antonio Trocolli, another precandidate, declined to run as well. Alfonsín was then appointed candidate of the UCR for the 1983 general elections, with Víctor Martínez as the candidate for the vice-presidency. The UCR proposed Alfonsín to run with De la Rúa as the candidate for the vice-presidency, to secure the conservative votes, but Alfonsín was confident to win the elections without help. The publicity was managed by David Ratto, who created the slogan "Ahora Alfonsín" (Spanish: "Now Alfonsín"), and the gesture of shaking hands. His campaign used a non-confrontational approach, in stark contrast with the Peronist candidate for the governorship of the Buenos Aires province, Herminio Iglesias. Iglesias burned a coffin with the seals of the UCR on live television, which generated a political scandal. Both Iglesias and Ítalo Luder, the Peronist candidate for the presidency, saw a decrease in their public image as a result. A group of UCR supporters drew graffiti that praised Alfonsín manliness and mocked Luder as effeminate; Alfonsín ordered to remove the graffitis as soon as he knew about them. During the campaign, both parties made similar proposals to reduce authoritarianism and the political influence of the military, and to maintain the Argentine claim in the Falkland Islands sovereignty dispute. Alfonsín denounced a pact between the military and the Peronist unions that sought an amnesty for the military. He maintained that the armed forces should be subject to the civilian government and that unions should be regulated. He also proposed an investigation into the actions of the military during the Dirty War. He closed his campaign by reading the preamble of the constitution of Argentina. The last rally was at the Plaza de la República, and was attended by 400,000 people. Opinion polls placed the UCR behind the PJ, but also placed Alfonsín as the most popular politician at the time. The elections were held on 30 October. The Alfonsín–Martínez ticket won with 51.7% of the vote, followed by Luder–Bittel with 40.1%. It was the first time since the rise of Juan Domingo Perón that the Peronist party was defeated in elections without electoral fraud or proscription. The UCR won 128 seats in the Assembly, forming a majority; and 18 seats in the Senate, constituting a minority. 18 provinces elected radical governors and 17 elected governors from either the Justicialist or local parties. Alfonsín took office on 10 December and gave a speech from the Buenos Aires Cabildo. The presidential inauguration of Alfonsín was attended by Isabel Perón. Despite internal recriminations for the defeat, the Peronist party agreed to support Alfonsín as president, to prevent a return of the military. There were still factions in the military ambitious to keep an authoritarian government, and groups such as the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo seeking reparations for the actions of the military during the Dirty War. Three days after taking office, Alfonsín sent a bill to Congress to revoke the self-amnesty law established by the military. This made it possible for the judiciary to investigate the crimes committed during the Dirty War. During the campaign, Alfonsín had promised that he would do this while Luder had been non-committal. Alfonsín also ordered the initiation of judicial cases against guerrilla leaders Mario Firmenich, Fernando Vaca Narvaja, Ricardo Obregón Cano, Rodolfo Galimberti, Roberto Perdía, Héctor Pardo and Enrique Gorriarán Merlo; and military leaders Jorge Videla, Emilio Massera, Orlando Agosti, Roberto Viola, Armando Lambruschini, Omar Graffigna, Leopoldo Galtieri, Jorge Anaya and Basilio Lami Dozo. He also requested the extradition of guerrilla leaders who were living abroad. Most of the first cabinet, organized in Chascomús, was composed of trusted colleagues of Alfonsín. Alfonsín appointed as minister of labor Antonio Mucci, who belonged to a faction of the UCR that sought to reduce the influence of Peronism among labor unions, and promptly sent a bill to Congress designed to promote independent unions. Facing an economic crisis, he appointed Bernardo Grinspun as minister of the economy. He appointed Aldo Neri minister of health, Dante Caputo minister of foreign relations, Antonio Tróccoli minister of interior affairs, Roque Carranza minister of public works, Carlos Alconada Aramburu minister of education, and Raúl Borrás minister of defense. Juan Carlos Pugliese led the Chamber of Deputies, and Edison Otero was the provisional President of the Senate. Many presidential negotiations took place at the Quinta de Olivos, the official residence of the president, rather than at the Casa Rosada. The priority of Raúl Alfonsín was to consolidate democracy, incorporate the armed forces into their standard role in a civilian government, and prevent further military coups. Alfonsín first tried to reduce the political power of the military with budget cuts, reductions of military personnel and changing their political tasks. As for the crimes committed during the Dirty War, Alfonsín was willing to respect the command responsibility and accept the "superior orders" defense for the military of lower ranks, as long as the Junta leaders were sentenced under military justice. This project was resisted by human rights organizations such as Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo and public opinion, as it was expected that the defendants would be acquitted or receive low sentences. The military considered that the Dirty War was legally sanctioned, and considered the prosecutions to be unjustified. Alfonsín also established the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons (CONADEP), composed of several well-known personalities, to document cases of forced disappearances, human rights violations and abduction of children. Alfonsín sent a military code bill to Congress so that the military would use it. In its "Nunca más" report (Spanish: Never again), the CONADEP revealed the wide scope of the crimes committed during the Dirty War, and how the Supreme Council of the military had supported the military's actions against the guerrillas. As a result, Alfonsín sponsored the Trial of the Juntas, in which, for the first time, the leaders of a military coup in Argentina were on trial. The first hearings began at the Supreme Court in April 1985 and lasted for the remainder of the year. In December, the tribunal handed down life sentences for Jorge Videla and former Navy Chief Emilio Massera, as well as 17-year sentences for.

It was expected that the defendants in the Dirty War prosecutions would be acquitted or receive light sentences, as the military viewed the conflict as legally sanctioned and considered the trials unjustified. President Alfonsín established the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons (CONADEP), composed of prominent figures, to document forced disappearances, human rights violations, and the abduction of children. He introduced a military code bill to Congress to regulate military conduct. The "Nunca más" report by CONADEP revealed the extensive nature of the crimes and how the Supreme Council of the military supported its actions against guerrillas. Alfonsín sponsored the Trial of the Juntas, marking the first time military coup leaders were prosecuted; the first hearings began at the Supreme Court in April 1985 and continued through the year. In December, Jorge Videla and Emilio Massera received life sentences, and Roberto Eduardo Viola was sentenced to 17 years; President Leopoldo Galtieri was acquitted of repression charges but was court-martialed in May 1986 for malfeasance during the Falklands War; Ramón Camps received a 25-year sentence. The trials also included Mario Firmenich, captured in Brazil in 1984 and extradited in 1984, and José López Rega, extradited from Miami in 1986 due to his ties with the Argentine Anticommunist Alliance. The military was supported by the families of subversion victims, a group formed to counter the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo, though it had few followers. The trials were followed by bomb attacks, rumors of military protests, and a possible coup. Alfonsín sought to calm the military by increasing their budget, but when that failed, he proposed the Full Stop Law, setting a deadline for Dirty War-related prosecutions. Congress approved the law despite strong public opposition. Prosecutors filed 487 charges against 300 officers, including 100 still in active service. Major Ernesto Barreiro refused to appear in court and initiated a mutiny in Córdoba; Lieutenant Colonel Aldo Rico launched another mutiny at Campo de Mayo, supporting Barreiro. The rebels were known as "Carapintadas" due to their use of military camouflage. The CGT called a general strike in support of Alfonsín, and large crowds gathered in the Plaza de Mayo. Alfonsín negotiated directly with the rebels and secured their surrender, announcing the end of the crisis from the Casa Rosada balcony. The mutineers eventually surrendered, but the government proceeded with the Law of Due Obedience to regulate the trials. The timing of both events was exploited by the military, and opposition parties described the outcome as a surrender by Alfonsín. Aldo Rico escaped from prison in January 1988 and launched a new mutiny in a distant northeast regiment; this time, military support and public outcry were minimal. The army attacked him, and Rico surrendered after brief combat. Colonel Mohamed Alí Seineldín launched another mutiny in late 1988; the mutineers were defeated and jailed, but the military avoided opening fire. Alfonsín’s goal of reconciling the military with the civilian population failed, as the public rejected military complaints and the military focused on internal issues. The Movimiento Todos por la Patria, a small guerrilla group led by Enrique Gorriarán Merlo, attacked the Regiment of La Tablada in 1989; the army killed many members and quickly defeated the uprising. During his presidency, Alfonsín clashed with labor unions over economic reforms and trade liberalization, as Peronism still controlled the unions, the most powerful in Latin America, with the General Confederation of Labour (CGT) being the largest. Alfonsín sought to reduce Peronist influence, rejecting single-candidate internal elections, which he deemed totalitarian, and proposing changes to election laws, removal of dictatorship-appointed union leaders, and new elections. The CGT rejected the proposal as interventionist, prompting Peronist politicians to oppose it. The law passed the Chamber of Deputies but failed in the Senate by one vote. A second bill calling only for elections without government supervision was approved, leaving unions Peronist. The CGT was internally divided: Lorenzo Miguel, aligned with the Justicialist party, led "the 62 organizations" faction; Saúl Ubaldini, more confrontational and distrustful of PJ politicians, became secretary general; his lack of political ties enabled him to mediate between factions. Carlos Alderete led a faction closer to Alfonsín, known as "the 15" unions. The government sought to deepen divisions by appointing Alderete as minister of labor and promoting legislation favoring his faction; he was removed after the 1987 midterm election defeat, but the government maintained good relations with his faction. Alfonsín maintained a dictatorship-era regulation allowing wage regulation, authorizing wage increases every three months to match inflation. The CGT rejected this, proposing instead free negotiations. Alfonsín allowed strikes, previously forbidden during the dictatorship, giving unions another avenue to expand influence. There were thirteen general strikes and thousands of minor labor conflicts. Unlike past situations, the CGT supported Alfonsín during military rebellions and did not back removing a non-Peronist president. The conflicts stemmed from high inflation, prompting unions to demand higher wages, with support from non-unionized retirees, the church, and left-wing factions. Popular support enabled the government to endure despite union opposition. After the end of the military dictatorship, Alfonsín promoted cultural and educational reforms to reduce authoritarianism and supported press freedom. Many intellectuals and scientists who had left the country returned, improving university quality, with the University of Buenos Aires regaining 1960s standards. Many intellectuals entered politics, enriching political discourse, benefiting both Alfonsín and Peronist Antonio Cafiero. Divorce was legalized in 1987; the church opposed it, but it had broad popular support, including Catholic factions who argued that marital separation already existed and divorce merely formalized it. The church opposed Alfonsín afterward and successfully pressured to prevent the abolition of religious education. In line with Pope John Paul II’s teachings, the church criticized rising drug use, terrorism, abortion, and pornography. Alfonsín intended to decriminalize abortion but abandoned the idea to avoid further conflict with the church. Argentina had a tense relationship with the United Kingdom due to the Falklands War; the UK temporarily banned foreign ships from entering the exclusion zone in 1986. Argentina responded with air and marine patrols and military exercises in Patagonia, but this did not satisfy military hard-liners. Alfonsín proposed postponing sovereignty discussions and instead negotiating a de jure cease of hostilities, reduced military forces, and normalized relations with the UK. The UK did not trust the proposal, suspecting it was a cover for sovereignty talks. The Beagle conflict with Chile remained unresolved despite 1978 Papal mediation. The military, disturbed by the juntas trial, rejected the proposed agreement and continued claiming the islands. Alfonsín called for a referendum to settle the dispute. Despite opposition from the military and the Justicialist party, which urged abstention, support reached 82%. The bill passed the Senate by a single vote, as the PJ resisted. The Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1984 between Chile and Argentina was signed the following year, ending the conflict. Human rights violations by Chilean President Augusto Pinochet and revelations of Chilean support for British forces during the Falklands War remained contentious. The Argentine church invited Pope John Paul II for a second visit in 1987 to celebrate his successful mediation; he celebrated World Youth Day near the Obelisk of Buenos Aires and gave a mass at the Basilica of Our Lady of Luján. Argentina allied with Brazil, Uruguay, and Peru—countries that had recently ended military dictatorships—to mediate the U.S.-Nicaragua conflict. They formed the Contadora support group, which later shifted focus to foreign debt and diplomacy with the UK regarding the Falklands. Initially, Alfonsín refused to establish diplomatic relations with the Brazilian military government, doing so only after its end and José Sarney’s presidency. Their initial concern was increasing trade. The two presidents met in Foz do Iguaçu and issued a joint declaration on peaceful nuclear use. A second meeting in Buenos Aires strengthened trade agreements. Argentina and Brazil signed the Program of Integration and Economic Cooperation (PICE), and in 1988, with Uruguay, agreed to create a common market, leading to the 1991 Treaty of Asunción establishing Mercosur. Alfonsín was the first Argentine head of state to visit the USSR. He began his term facing severe economic problems: the economy had contracted by 15% in the previous decade, foreign debt was nearly $43 billion, and the country narrowly avoided sovereign default in 1982. In 1982, GDP fell by 5.6% and manufacturing profits by 55%; unemployment was nearly 10%, inflation nearly 209%, and foreign investment seemed unlikely. The country had a $6.7 billion deficit. Possible solutions like currency devaluation, privatization, or import restrictions would have been unpopular. Initially, the government took no strong action. Bernardo Grinspun, the first minister of economy, raised wages to 1975 levels, causing inflation to reach 32%. He failed to secure favorable foreign debt terms and, risking default, negotiated with the IMF, which demanded spending cuts. International credits prevented default by the end of 1984, but Grinspun resigned in March 1985 when debt reached $1 billion and the IMF denied further credits. He was succeeded by Juan Vital Sourrouille, who introduced the Austral plan in 1985. The plan froze prices and wages, stopped money printing, implemented spending cuts, and introduced the Austral, worth 1 USD. The plan succeeded short-term in curbing inflation. However, by this point, most of Alfonsín’s initial popularity had declined, and he could not convince many of the long-term benefits of austerity. Inflation rose again by year-end, the CGT opposed the wage freeze, and the business community opposed the price freeze. Alfonsín believed privatization and deregulation might work, but both the PJ and his own party opposed them. The Austral plan was undermined by populist economic policies. With World Bank support, the government tried new measures in 1987, including tax increases, privatizations, and spending cuts. These could not be enforced; the government lost the 1987 midterm elections, the "15" unions distanced themselves, and the business community offered no clear path. The PJ, aiming for a 1989 presidential victory, opposed measures it saw as socially harmful. The "Spring plan" aimed to stabilize the economy until the elections by freezing prices and wages and reducing the federal deficit. It had a worse reception than the Austral plan and received no party support. The World Bank and IMF refused to extend credits; big exporters refused to sell dollars to the Central Bank, depleting reserves. The austral was devalued in February 1989, and inflation turned into hyperinflation. The US dollar was worth 14 australes at the beginning of 1989 and 17,000 by May. The 1989 presidential elections occurred during the crisis, and Justicialist Carlos Menem won. By winter 1989, inflation was so severe that Alfonsín transferred power to Menem on 8 July, five months earlier than scheduled. Alfonsín remained president of the UCR after leaving office, staying until the party’s defeat in the 1991 legislative elections. Damaged by the 1989 hyperinflation, the UCR lost in several districts. Alfonsín returned as party president in 1993. He supported a special budget for Buenos Aires, led by governor Eduardo Duhalde. Radical legislator Leopoldo Moreau supported the budget more strongly than the Peronists. Both parties formed an informal alliance in the province. Alfonsín also supported a constitutional amendment allowing Duhalde to run for re-election. President Menem sought a constitutional amendment to allow his re-election, which Alfonsín opposed. The 1993 midterm victory strengthened the PJ, which approved the bill in the Senate. Menem proposed a referendum to force radical deputies to support it and introduced a bill allowing a constitutional amendment with a simple majority in Congress. As a result, Alfonsín signed the Pact of Olivos with Menem. Under the pact, the UCR would support Menem’s proposal with amendments reducing presidential power. The Council of Magistracy reduced executive influence over the judiciary, Buenos Aires became an autonomous territory with elected mayor, and the presidential term was reduced to four years. The election system adopted a two-round system, and the electoral college was abolished. Alfonsín was elected to the constituent assembly that drafted the 1994 constitutional amendment. A faction of the UCR, led by Fernando de la Rúa, opposed the pact, but the party as a whole supported Alfonsín. The UCR received only 19% of the vote in the 1995 elections, finishing third behind Frepaso when Menem was re-elected. Alfonsín resigned as party president in that year. Raúl Alfonsín made the Pact of Olivos with President Carlos Menem, leading the UCR to support Menem's constitutional amendment proposals with modifications that reduced presidential power. These changes included limiting executive influence over the judiciary, granting the city of Buenos Aires autonomy to elect its mayor, and shortening the presidential term to four years. The presidential election system was changed to include a two-round system, and the electoral college was abolished. Alfonsín was elected to the constituent assembly that drafted the 1994 constitutional amendment. A faction of the UCR, led by Fernando de la Rúa, opposed the pact, but the party as a whole backed Alfonsín. In the 1995 presidential elections, the UCR received only 19% of the vote, finishing third behind the Frepaso, and Alfonsín resigned as party president that year. The UCR and Frepaso formed the Alliance for Work, Justice, and Education, led by Alfonsín, de la Rúa, and Rodolfo Terragno from the UCR, and Carlos Álvarez and Graciela Fernández Meijide from the Frepaso, which won the 1997 legislative elections. Alfonsín disagreed with de la Rúa on the fixed exchange rate, believing it had become harmful to the economy despite its past benefits. In 1999, Alfonsín suffered a car crash on Route 6 in Río Negro province during a campaign for governor Pablo Verani, was ejected from the vehicle due to not wearing a seat belt, and was hospitalized for 39 days. De la Rúa won the 1999 presidential election, defeating Eduardo Duhalde, the governor of Buenos Aires. Alfonsín was elected Senator for Buenos Aires Province in October 2001. When de la Rúa resigned during the December 2001 riots, Congress appointed Adolfo Rodríguez Saá, who also resigned, and Alfonsín instructed Radical legislators to support Duhalde as president, appointing him with ministers Horacio Jaunarena for Defense and Jorge Vanossi for Justice, helping Duhalde surpass the ambitions of Carlos Ruckauf and José Manuel de la Sota. Later in the year, due to health issues, Alfonsín stepped down, being replaced by Diana Conti. In 2006, Alfonsín supported a UCR faction advocating for an independent candidate in the 2007 presidential election, and the party endorsed Roberto Lavagna, a center-left economist who led Argentina’s economic recovery from 2002 until his departure from President Néstor Kirchner in December 2005; Lavagna finished in third place. On 1 October 2008, President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner honored Alfonsín with a bust at the Casa Rosada, marking his last public appearance. Alfonsín died at home on 31 March 2009 at age 82 after being diagnosed with lung cancer a year earlier. Hundreds gathered around his house on Santa Fe avenue, starting a candlelight vigil. Radical Julio Cobos, Fernández de Kirchner’s vice president, served as acting president and declared three days of national mourning. A ceremony in Congress, where his body was displayed in the Blue Hall, was attended by nearly a thousand people; his widow María Lorenza Barreneche could not attend due to poor health. The event was attended by former presidents Carlos Menem, Fernando de la Rúa, Eduardo Duhalde, and Néstor Kirchner, all Supreme Court justices, mayor Mauricio Macri, governor Daniel Scioli, Uruguayan president Tabaré Vázquez, and other politicians. The coffin was moved to La Recoleta Cemetery, where he was buried next to Leandro N. Alem, Hipólito Yrigoyen, and Arturo Illia. Perú and Paraguay declared national mourning, with Brazil, Chile, Colombia, France, Mexico, Paraguay, Peru, Spain, Uruguay, and the United States sending messages of condolence. Julio María Sanguinetti of Uruguay and Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil also attended the ceremony. Historians Félix Luna, Miguel Ángel de Marco, and Fernando Rocchi praise Alfonsín for his role in ending the Dirty War and restoring democracy, with Luna calling him an effective president who avoided using state power for personal gain. De Marco notes that the period was delicate, and any error could have led to a coup, though all three historians disagree on the Pact of Olivos: Luna sees it as a necessary compromise to prevent chaos, while De Marco and Rocchi view it as the greatest mistake of Alfonsín’s career. Alfonsín received the 1985 Princess of Asturias Award for international cooperation for resolving the Beagle dispute and restoring democracy. He was named "Illustrious Citizen of Buenos Aires Province" in 2008 and "Illustrious Citizen of Buenos Aires" in 2009, the latter posthumously received by his son Ricardo Alfonsín, ambassador to Spain.
